title: Do one third and two sixths of a strip reach the same place?
description: Two paper strips of the same length are folded, one into three equal parts and one into six, and one third and two sixths are shaded. Laying the sixth pieces on the third piece shows where the two shaded lengths end, and Keeko doubts it because two pieces seem more than one.
teaching_notes: One idea: to compare two fractions on strips, compare the lengths shaded and not the number of pieces. Watch for students who think two pieces are always more than one piece.

source: Using paper strips, check whether 1/3 and 2/6 are equivalent
video_script.why: The child checks with two folded strips that one third and two sixths are the same length, so they are equivalent fractions.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own check of one third and two sixths with paper strips
video_script.anchor: two paper strips of the same length, one folded into thirds and one into sixths
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says two sixths is more because two pieces are more than one piece. Laying one sixth piece on the third piece shows it covers only half of it, so counting pieces is not enough when the pieces differ in size.
video_script.payoff_line: One third and two sixths are the same length

final_answer.spoken: yes, one third and two sixths are equivalent

video_script.fraction_reading: one third, two sixths, one sixth
maths_rules: strip 1 folded into 3 equal parts, 1 part marked: 1/3
strip 2 folded into 6 equal parts, 2 parts marked: 2/6
each third is made of 2 sixths, so 2 pieces of 1/6 fit exactly on 1 piece of 1/3
so the two marked lengths are equal: 2/6 = 1/3
slip: Keeko thinks 2/6 is more because 2 pieces are more than 1 piece; one piece of 1/6 is only half of one piece of 1/3
video_script.design: One idea: compare the marked lengths, not the number of pieces. The two strips stay one above the other with left ends lined up.

<bookmark mark='fold'/>One strip is folded into three equal parts, and the other into six equal parts.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>We shade one third on the first strip and two sixths on the second.
Are one third and two sixths equivalent fractions?

That marked part is one third.

narration: <bookmark mark='lay'/>Step three, lay two sixth pieces on the third piece, because laying them together compares lengths.
<bookmark mark='end'/>Each third is made of two sixths, so both marked lengths end at the same place.
<bookmark mark='pay'/>One third and two sixths are the same length.
The two fractions are equivalent, and two sixths is one third.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks two sixths is more, because two pieces are more than one piece.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But one sixth piece covers only part of the third piece.
Counting pieces is not enough when the pieces are of different sizes.
